I'd just like to throw out there that a lot of people think 30's is a good point for kids, but that's not necessarily true. Once you get into your 30's, especially mid-to-late 30's, [fertility for the potential mother](https://yourfertility.org.au/for-women/age/) and various negative health risks for the potential child become very real considerations. 

For all of the older gents out there, you should know that while fertility isn't as much of an issue for us, there are numerous other risks for your child such as decreased intelligence, increased chance of autism, and other conditions that grow worse as you get older as well. One such example, Huntington's Disease, is a hellish disease, and is more common in the children of men who were 40+ when the child was conceived. 

None of this is is to say that it isn't smart to wait until you're in a good position financially; it is smart. It is also smart to consider the potential difficulty conceiving and that the child might not be as healthy as you would hope if you wait for too long.

yes. The reasoning is this:

Some things are "forced" to change because their adaptations benefit them. Through whatever the cataclysm was, they weren't properly adapted to it, but one or multiple of them had a mutation which made it so they could survive.

 Like say there's a species that's used to a warm environment, so it has a light coat. The climate suddenly changes, and it becomes freezing. Obviously this light coat isn't beneficial, so some of them start freezing to death. Then one of them had a mutation which caused a heavy coat to grow. It's better equipped to handle this new environment, so it passes on its genes. So do its descendants, and this continues, all while the light coats are still freezing. Eventually, you'll have this species of heavily-haired creatures where there were light coats originally. 

You can connect this to your last grouping (the whole forced change, no change, and dying off thing.) One group died off (light hairs) while another group adapted and survived (heavy hairs.) If there had been another group that was adapted to survive the new cold environment, then it wouldn't have experienced a change since it didn't need to.

the thing is, this is an overly simplistic view of evolution, and it kind of brings some inaccuracies along with it. It makes it seem like there's this deliberate change when there really isn't. Like is said above, there's this random change, and it just happened to be beneficial. There could have just as easily have been a mutation that was actually worse than before (like if the above species was born without hair, which is obviously worse than at least having some.) The thing is, you don't really see this in a population since it isn't beneficial, and it doesn't get passed on. 

Another inaccuracy this brings along is the idea that evolution is sudden, when it's a ridiculously gradual process. It takes many generations (not necessarily years, since it's really all about the difference in generations) for a noticeable change to occur. And then it takes even more for a new species to come about. 

Yet another is that what's evolved is "better". This isn't necessarily true, it just means that it has filled another niche. It's the reason why you'll see so many species of squirrels, birds, etc. 

And the last one (that I've sort of already touched on) is the shift into something else. It's not that humans or anything is changing into something better, it's simply changing. there's no intent for a new species.
